excerpt: We invest deeply in developing or adopting new science-backed evaluations that provide high precision and high recall indications of whether a covered system has reached a capability threshold in one of our Tracked Categories.
paraphrase: OpenAI invests in science-backed evaluations designed to accurately detect when a system reaches a capability threshold in a Tracked Category.

excerpt: Our evaluations are intended to approximate the full capability that the adversary contemplated by our threat model could extract from the deployment candidate model, including by using the highest-capability tier of system settings, using a version of the model that has a negligible rate of safety-based refusals on our Tracked Category capability evaluations (which may require a separate model variant), and with the best presently-available scaffolds.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to approximate the maximum capability an adversary could extract, using top-tier settings, low-refusal model variants, and best available scaffolding.

excerpt: These measures are taken to approximate the high end of expected elicitation by threat actors attempting to misuse the model, and should be tailored depending on the level of expected access (e.g., doing finetuning if the weights will be released).
paraphrase: These measures approximate the high end of expected misuse elicitation and should be tailored to the level of anticipated access, such as finetuning when weights are released.

excerpt: Nonetheless, given the continuous progress in model scaffolding and elicitation techniques, we regard any one-time capability elicitation in a frontier model as a lower bound, rather than a ceiling, on capabilities that may emerge in real world use and misuse.
paraphrase: Because scaffolding and elicitation techniques keep improving, a single capability test is treated as a floor, not a ceiling, on real-world capability.

excerpt: We incorporate this uncertainty into our assessments. We monitor the technical landscape for changes to the elicitation techniques and best practices, and reassess our evaluations as needed.
paraphrase: OpenAI factors this uncertainty into assessments and monitors the field to reassess evaluations as elicitation practices evolve.

excerpt: Capability evaluations come in two different forms:
paraphrase: There are two forms of capability evaluations.

context_stem: Capability evaluations come in two different forms:
excerpt: Scalable Evaluations: automated evaluations designed to measure proxies that approximate whether a capability threshold has been crossed. Scalable evaluations have associated "indicative thresholds," which are levels of performance that we have pre-determined to indicate that a deployment may have reached a capability threshold.
paraphrase: Scalable evaluations are automated proxy measures with pre-set indicative thresholds signaling a possible capability threshold crossing.

context_stem: Capability evaluations come in two different forms:
excerpt: Deep Dives: designed to provide additional evidence validating the scalable evaluations' findings on whether a capability threshold has been crossed. These may include a wide range of evidence gathering activities, such as human expert red-teaming, expert consultations, resource-intensive third party evaluations (e.g., bio wet lab studies, assessments by independent third party evaluators), and any other activity requested by SAG.
paraphrase: Deep Dives validate scalable evaluation findings through activities like red-teaming, expert consultation, and third-party evaluations, or other activities SAG requests.

section_heading: An example of a Tracked Category capability evaluation
excerpt: To assess the degree to which a covered system can reduce the barriers to creating a biological weapon, our current evaluations test both how capable the system is at providing useful information to someone creating a weapon and how capable it is of directly integrating with relevant tools, such as ordering precursor materials via the Internet.
paraphrase: The example describes testing a system's ability to lower barriers to bioweapon creation, both via informational assistance and tool integration like ordering precursors.

section_heading: An example of a Tracked Category capability evaluation
excerpt: Our evaluations test acquiring critical and sensitive information across the five stages of the biological threat creation process: Ideation, Acquisition, Magnification, Formulation, and Release. These evaluations, developed by domain experts, cover things like how to troubleshoot the laboratory processes involved.
paraphrase: The evaluations, built by domain experts, test information acquisition across five biological threat creation stages including lab troubleshooting.

section_heading: An example of a Tracked Category capability evaluation
excerpt: You can learn more about our Tracked Category capability evaluations in past system cards, such as those for OpenAI o1 and Operator.
paraphrase: More information on these evaluations is available in prior system cards, including for OpenAI o1 and Operator.

excerpt: The Preparedness Framework applies to any new or updated deployment that has a plausible chance of reaching a capability threshold whose corresponding risks are not addressed by an existing Safeguards Report.
paraphrase: The Framework covers any deployment plausibly reaching a capability threshold not already addressed by a Safeguards Report.

excerpt: Examples of such covered deployments are:
paraphrase: Lead-in listing examples of covered deployments.

context_stem: Examples of such covered deployments are:
excerpt: every frontier model (e.g., OpenAI o1 or OpenAI o3) that we plan to deploy externally
paraphrase: Any frontier model planned for external deployment is a covered deployment.

context_stem: Examples of such covered deployments are:
excerpt: any agentic system (including significant agents deployed only internally) that represents a substantial increase in the capability frontier
paraphrase: Agentic systems, including internal-only significant agents, that substantially increase capability are covered.

context_stem: Examples of such covered deployments are:
excerpt: any significant change in the deployment conditions of an existing model (e.g., enabling finetuning, releasing weights, or significant new features) that makes the existing Capabilities Report or Safeguards Report no longer reasonably applicable
paraphrase: Significant changes to deployment conditions that invalidate existing Capabilities or Safeguards Reports are covered.

context_stem: Examples of such covered deployments are:
excerpt: incremental updates or distilled models with unexpectedly significant increases in capability.
paraphrase: Incremental updates or distilled models showing unexpected significant capability increases are covered.

excerpt: If justified by our forecasts and threat models as potentially posing a severe risk during development and prior to external deployment, we will select an appropriate checkpoint during development to be covered by the Preparedness Framework.
paraphrase: When forecasts and threat models suggest severe risk during development, a development checkpoint will be selected for Framework coverage.

excerpt: In cases of ambiguity about whether a model is covered by the Preparedness Framework, the SAG is responsible for making the final determination.
paraphrase: SAG makes the final call when coverage under the Framework is ambiguous.

excerpt: Prior to deployment, every covered model undergoes the suite of Scalable Evaluations. The results of these evaluations, and any noteworthy observations that should affect interpretation of the results, are compiled into a Capabilities Report that is submitted to the SAG.
paraphrase: Covered models are put through Scalable Evaluations before deployment, with results compiled into a Capabilities Report submitted to SAG.

excerpt: The determination that a threshold has been reached is informed by these indicative results from capability evaluations, and also reflects holistic judgment based on the totality of available evidence – for example, information about the methodological robustness of evaluation results.
paraphrase: Threshold determinations combine indicative evaluation results with holistic judgment on all available evidence, including methodological robustness.

excerpt: The SAG reviews the Capabilities Report and decides on next steps. These can include:
paraphrase: SAG reviews the Capabilities Report and chooses among possible next steps.

context_stem: The SAG reviews the Capabilities Report and decides on next steps. These can include:
excerpt: Determine that the capability threshold has been crossed, and therefore recommend implementing and assessing corresponding safeguards, if they have not already been implemented and assessed.
paraphrase: SAG may determine a threshold was crossed and recommend implementing and assessing safeguards if not already done.

context_stem: The SAG reviews the Capabilities Report and decides on next steps. These can include:
excerpt: Determine that a threshold has not been crossed: If the scalable evaluations did not cross their indicative thresholds, the SAG may conclude that the model does not have High or Critical capability, and recommend no further action.
paraphrase: If scalable evaluations stay below indicative thresholds, SAG may conclude no High or Critical capability exists and recommend no further action.

excerpt: In general, models that we distill, fine-tune, or quantize from a model that was previously determined not to cross a High capability threshold will ordinarily not require additional safety measures barring reason to believe a significant increase in capability has occurred.
paraphrase: Derivative models from ones already below the High threshold usually don't need extra safety measures unless there's reason to suspect a significant capability increase.

context_stem: The SAG reviews the Capabilities Report and decides on next steps. These can include:
excerpt: Recommend deep dive research: This is appropriate if SAG needs additional evidence in order to make a recommendation.
paraphrase: SAG may recommend deep dive research when it needs more evidence before making a recommendation.

excerpt: Safeguards that mitigate the risk of severe harm are at the core of our safe deployment approach for covered systems that reach a capability threshold. This section describes the process through which we select which safeguards to apply and how we evaluate whether those safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: Safeguards mitigating severe harm risk are central to safe deployment; this section explains how safeguards are selected and assessed for sufficiency.

excerpt: If a covered system appears likely to cross a capability threshold, we will start to work on safeguards to sufficiently reduce the risks of severe harm associated with that threshold even if a formal capability determination has not yet been made.
paraphrase: Safeguard development begins as soon as a system appears likely to cross a threshold, even before formal determination.

excerpt: Each capability threshold has a corresponding class of risk-specific safeguard guidelines under the Preparedness Framework. We use the following process to select safeguards for a deployment:
paraphrase: Each threshold has associated safeguard guidelines, and a defined process is used to select safeguards for deployments.

context_stem: We use the following process to select safeguards for a deployment:
excerpt: We first identify the plausible ways in which the associated risk of severe harm can come to fruition in the proposed deployment.
paraphrase: The process begins by identifying plausible pathways by which severe harm risk could materialize.

context_stem: We use the following process to select safeguards for a deployment:
excerpt: For each of those, we then identify specific safeguards that either exist or should be implemented that would address the risk.
paraphrase: For each pathway, specific existing or needed safeguards addressing the risk are identified.

context_stem: We use the following process to select safeguards for a deployment:
excerpt: For each identified safeguard, we identify methods to measure their efficacy and an efficacy threshold.
paraphrase: Each safeguard has associated efficacy measurement methods and an efficacy threshold.

excerpt: We consider separate safeguards for two of the main ways in which risks can be realized: a malicious user, who can leverage the model to cause the severe harm, and a misaligned model, which autonomously causes the harm. We illustrate the types of safeguards for each in Table 3.
paraphrase: Safeguards are separately considered for malicious-user misuse and for autonomous misaligned-model harm, illustrated in Table 3.

excerpt: The methodology for security controls is similar, although focused on the relevant security threat models.
paraphrase: Security controls follow a similar methodology, tailored to relevant security threat models.

excerpt: Appendix C provides illustrative examples of potential safeguards and safeguard efficacy assessments that could be used to establish that we have sufficiently minimized the risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: Appendix C gives illustrative examples of safeguards and efficacy assessments relevant to demonstrating sufficient risk minimization.

excerpt: The examples aim to provide insight on our thinking but should not be construed as a definitive checklist of the safeguards we will apply to a given launch.
paraphrase: The examples illustrate reasoning but are not a definitive checklist for any particular launch.

excerpt: We compile the information on the planned safeguards needed to minimize the risk of severe harm into a Safeguards Report. The Safeguards Report should include the following information:
paraphrase: Planned safeguard information is compiled into a Safeguards Report, which should contain specified information.

context_stem: The Safeguards Report should include the following information:
excerpt: Identified ways a risk of severe harm can be realized for the given deployment, each mapped to the associated security controls and safeguards
paraphrase: The report identifies ways severe harm risk could be realized, each mapped to relevant controls and safeguards.

context_stem: The Safeguards Report should include the following information:
excerpt: Details about the efficacy of those safeguards
paraphrase: The report includes efficacy details of the safeguards.

context_stem: The Safeguards Report should include the following information:
excerpt: An assessment on the residual risk of severe harm based on the deployment
paraphrase: The report assesses residual severe harm risk given the deployment.

context_stem: The Safeguards Report should include the following information:
excerpt: Any notable limitations with the information provided
paraphrase: The report notes any significant limitations in the provided information.

excerpt: Many safeguards can be reused across different deployments, and so in practice we may find that the majority of deployments need few new safeguards and associated stress-testing beyond those already in place for prior deployments.
paraphrase: Because safeguards are often reusable, most deployments may need little new safeguard work beyond what already exists.

excerpt: SAG is responsible for assessing whether the safeguards associated with a given deployment sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm associated with the proposed deployment. The SAG will make this determination based on:
paraphrase: SAG assesses safeguard sufficiency for each deployment, basing its determination on specified factors.

context_stem: The SAG will make this determination based on:
excerpt: The level of capability in the Tracked Category based on the Capabilities Report.
paraphrase: One factor is the level of capability in the Tracked Category per the Capabilities Report.

context_stem: The SAG will make this determination based on:
excerpt: The associated risks of severe harm, as described in the threat model and where needed, advice of internal or external experts.
paraphrase: Another factor is the associated severe harm risks per the threat model, plus expert advice where needed.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against Malicious Users / Robustness
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against Malicious Users; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Robustness
excerpt: Robustness: Malicious users cannot use the model to cause the severe harm because they cannot elicit the necessary capability, such as because the model is modified to refuse to provide assistance to harmful tasks and is robust to jailbreaks that would circumvent those refusals.
paraphrase: A robustness claim asserts malicious users cannot elicit necessary capability due to refusal behavior and jailbreak resistance.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against Malicious Users / Usage Monitoring
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against Malicious Users; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Usage Monitoring
excerpt: Usage Monitoring: If a model does not refuse and provides assistance to harmful tasks, monitors can stop or catch malicious users before they have achieved an unacceptable scale of harm, through a combination of automated and human detection and enforcement within an acceptable time frame.
paraphrase: A usage monitoring claim asserts that detection and enforcement can stop malicious users before harm reaches unacceptable scale, even if the model assists.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against Malicious Users / Trust-based Access
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against Malicious Users; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Trust-based Access
excerpt: Trust-based Access: The actors who gain access to the model are not going to use it in a way that presents an associated risk of severe harm under our threat model.
paraphrase: A trust-based access claim asserts that authorized actors will not misuse the model in a way presenting severe harm risk.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model / Lack of Autonomous Capability
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Lack of Autonomous Capability
excerpt: Lack of Autonomous Capability: The model is not capable of carrying out tasks autonomously, including the risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: A lack-of-autonomous-capability claim asserts the model cannot autonomously carry out tasks including severe harm.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model / Value Alignment
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Value Alignment
excerpt: Value Alignment: The model consistently applies human values in novel settings (without any instructions) to avoid taking actions that cause harm, and has shown sufficiently minimal indications of misaligned behaviors like deception or scheming.
paraphrase: A value alignment claim asserts the model consistently applies human values in novel settings and shows minimal deception or scheming.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model / Instruction Alignment
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Instruction Alignment
excerpt: Instruction Alignment: The model consistently understands and follows user or system instructions, even when vague, and those instructions rule out pathways to causing severe harm.
paraphrase: An instruction alignment claim asserts the model reliably follows instructions, even vague ones, in ways that preclude severe harm pathways.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model / Reliable and Robust System Oversight
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model; Row: Potential claims; Sub: Reliable and Robust System Oversight
excerpt: Reliable and Robust System Oversight: Effective AI and human oversight of model actions detects and prevents execution of harm or subversion of safeguards.
paraphrase: A system oversight claim asserts effective AI and human oversight detects and prevents harm execution or safeguard subversion.

locator: Table 3 / Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model / System Architecture
context_stem: Column: Safeguards Against a Misaligned Model; Row: Potential claims; Sub: System Architecture
excerpt: System Architecture: The model can't take actions that cause harm because it lacks access to output channels or mechanisms to persist sufficiently to execute the harm, due to system design and restricted permissions.
paraphrase: A system architecture claim asserts the model lacks the output channels or persistence mechanisms needed to execute harm, by design.

excerpt: Table 3: Types of safeguards. See Appendix C.1 and C.2 for additional details.
paraphrase: Caption noting the table describes safeguard types with further detail in Appendix C.1 and C.2.

context_stem: The SAG will make this determination based on:
excerpt: The safeguards in place and their effectiveness based on the Safeguards Report.
paraphrase: Another factor is current safeguards and their effectiveness per the Safeguards Report.

context_stem: The SAG will make this determination based on:
excerpt: The baseline risk from other deployments, based on a review of any non-OpenAI deployments of models which have crossed the capability thresholds and any public evidence of the safeguards applied for those models.
paraphrase: Another factor is baseline risk from other developers' deployments that crossed thresholds and public evidence of their safeguards.

excerpt: Covered systems that reach High capability must have safeguards that sufficiently minimize the associated risk of severe harm before they are deployed.
paraphrase: Systems reaching High capability must have sufficient safeguards before deployment.

excerpt: Systems that reach Critical capability also require safeguards that sufficiently minimize associated risks during development.
paraphrase: Systems reaching Critical capability also need sufficient safeguards during development, not just deployment.

excerpt: Based on this evidence, SAG then has the following decision points:
paraphrase: SAG has several possible decision points based on the evidence.

context_stem: SAG then has the following decision points:
excerpt: SAG can find that it is confident that the safeguards sufficiently minimize the associated risk of severe harm for the proposed deployment, and recommend deployment.
paraphrase: SAG may find safeguards sufficient and recommend deployment.

context_stem: SAG then has the following decision points:
excerpt: SAG can request further evaluation of the effectiveness of the safeguards to evaluate if the associated risk of severe harm is sufficiently minimized
paraphrase: SAG may request further evaluation of safeguard effectiveness before determining sufficiency.

context_stem: SAG then has the following decision points:
excerpt: SAG can find the safeguards do not sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm and recommend potential alternative deployment conditions or additional or more effective safeguards that would sufficiently minimize the risk.
paraphrase: SAG may find safeguards insufficient and recommend alternative conditions or stronger safeguards.

excerpt: The SAG will strive to recommend further actions that are as targeted and non-disruptive as possible while still mitigating risks of severe harm.
paraphrase: SAG aims to make recommendations that are minimally disruptive while still mitigating severe harm risk.

excerpt: All of SAG's recommendations will go to OpenAI Leadership for final decision-making in accordance with the decision-making practices outlined in Appendix B.
paraphrase: SAG recommendations go to OpenAI Leadership for final decisions per Appendix B practices.

excerpt: We expect to continuously improve our safeguards over time.
paraphrase: OpenAI expects to keep improving safeguards over time.

excerpt: If we find reasonable evidence that our safeguards are not working as expected, we will validate the information being received and review the sufficiency of our safeguards.
paraphrase: If evidence suggests safeguards are underperforming, the information will be validated and safeguard sufficiency reviewed.

excerpt: We recognize that another frontier AI model developer might develop or release a system with High or Critical capability in one of this Framework's Tracked Categories and may do so without instituting comparable safeguards to the ones we have committed to.
paraphrase: OpenAI acknowledges other developers might release High or Critical capability systems without comparable safeguards.

excerpt: Such an action could significantly increase the baseline risk of severe harm being realized in the world, and limit the degree to which we can reduce risk using our safeguards.
paraphrase: Such actions by others could raise baseline severe harm risk and limit how much OpenAI's own safeguards can reduce it.

excerpt: If we are able to rigorously confirm that such a scenario has occurred, then we could adjust accordingly the level of safeguards that we require in that capability area, but only if:
paraphrase: If such a scenario is rigorously confirmed, OpenAI could adjust required safeguard levels in that area, subject to conditions.

context_stem: we could adjust accordingly the level of safeguards that we require in that capability area, but only if:
excerpt: we assess that doing so does not meaningfully increase the overall risk of severe harm,
paraphrase: Condition: the adjustment must not meaningfully increase overall severe harm risk.

context_stem: we could adjust accordingly the level of safeguards that we require in that capability area, but only if:
excerpt: we publicly acknowledge that we are making the adjustment,
paraphrase: Condition: the adjustment must be publicly acknowledged.

context_stem: we could adjust accordingly the level of safeguards that we require in that capability area, but only if:
excerpt: and, in order to avoid a race to the bottom on safety, we keep our safeguards at a level more protective than the other AI developer, and share information to validate this claim.
paraphrase: Condition: safeguards must remain more protective than the other developer's, with information shared to validate this.

section_heading: 4.4 Increasing safeguards before internal use and further development
excerpt: Models that have reached or are forecasted to reach Critical capability in a Tracked Category present severe dangers and should be treated with extreme caution.
paraphrase: Models at or forecast to reach Critical capability present severe dangers requiring extreme caution.

section_heading: 4.4 Increasing safeguards before internal use and further development
excerpt: Such models require additional safeguards (safety and security controls) during development, regardless of whether or when they are externally deployed.
paraphrase: Critical-capability models need additional safety and security controls during development, regardless of external deployment timing.

section_heading: 4.4 Increasing safeguards before internal use and further development
excerpt: We do not currently possess any models that have Critical levels of capability, and we expect to further update this Preparedness Framework before reaching such a level with any model.
paraphrase: OpenAI currently has no Critical-capability models and expects to update this Framework before any model reaches that level.

section_heading: 4.4 Increasing safeguards before internal use and further development
excerpt: Our approach to Critical capabilities will need to be robust to both malicious actors (either internal or external) and model misalignment risks.
paraphrase: The approach to Critical capabilities must address both malicious actor threats (internal or external) and model misalignment risks.

section_heading: 4.4 Increasing safeguards before internal use and further development
excerpt: The SAG retains discretion over when to request deep dive evaluations of models whose scalable evaluations indicate that they may possess or may be nearing critical capability thresholds.
paraphrase: SAG has discretion to request deep dive evaluations for models whose scalable evaluations suggest possible or nearing Critical capability.
